Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent

Qiaoyu Zheng Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China      Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory, Shanghai, China    Weike Zhao Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China      Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory, Shanghai, China    Yanjie Fan Affiliation: Xinhua Hospital affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China    Ye Cao Affiliation: Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, The Chinese University of Hong Kong    Mengqi Jiang Affiliation: Department of Radiation Oncology, Shanghai Chest Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China    Xiao Zhou Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Xiaoman Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Pengcheng Qiu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Yongguo Yu Affiliation: Xinhua Hospital affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China    Yanfeng Wang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Ya Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Chaoyi Wu Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China         Weidi Xie Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China      Affiliation: Corresponding authors. Email addresses: {three-world, ya_zhang, wtzxxxwcy02, weidi}@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract

Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1%, 57.8%, 64.4% versus 15.6%, 31.1%, 20.0% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

1 INTRODUCTION

Genomic analysis has become an increasingly central component of modern precision medicine, particularly in rare disease and cancer [1, 2, 3]. Advances in high-throughput sequencing have enabled the systematic characterization of genetic variation at unprecedented scale, facilitating molecular diagnosis, disease classification, patient stratification, and the identification of targeted therapeutic opportunities [4, 5, 2, 3]. Yet, as sequencing has become increasingly accessible, the major bottleneck in genomic medicine has shifted from data generation to the interpretation of genetic variation and the derivation of clinically actionable insights [6, 7, 8, 9], a challenge famously framed as the “$1,000 genome, $100,000 analysis” [10].

This bottleneck arises from three challenges: (i) fragmented evidence: relevant knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous and often siloed sources, including variant databases, biomedical literature, clinical guidelines, and patient phenotypes; (ii) expertise-intensive reasoning: assessing variant significance demands substantial domain knowledge and contextual judgment involving disease mechanisms, inheritance patterns, phenotypic context, and evidence strength; and (iii) dynamic analytical workflows: different patients and questions entail adaptive combinations of variant annotation, phenotype matching, evidence retrieval, pathogenicity assessment, and result synthesis. As a result, although conventional bioinformatics tools can automate individual steps [11, 12], performing a comprehensive genomic analysis still relies heavily on experts to integrate disparate information and synthesize actionable conclusions, limiting its scalability.

Recently, large language model (LLM)-based agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for automating similar knowledge-intensive clinical tasks by combining reasoning with information retrieval and tool use [13, 14]. Bringing this paradigm to genomic analysis, however, is non-trivial. The field relies on a vast and continuously evolving ecosystem of professional guidelines, databases, and computational tools, each with distinct formats, interfaces, and usage protocols [15, 16]. Systematically translating these heterogeneous resources into standardized, agent-operable capabilities within a unified, scalable “agent harness” is therefore a central design problem [17]. Crucially, such a harness must preserve the flexibility of LLMs to dynamically compose workflows for diverse clinical questions, while ensuring that individual analyses follow established domain-specific procedures and standards.

Here, we present ClinGeX, a skill-centred agentic framework designed to support and accelerate clinical genomic analysis across heterogeneous inputs, including free text, pedigree images, clinical documents and sequencing data. ClinGeX comprises 105 specialized skills, each encoding an atomic operation in clinical genomics. These skills span five recurring categories: guideline following, entity mapping, data-source lookup, numerical calculation and model-based prediction. In the deployed system, they are grouped by operational role into three functional classes—guide, search and analysis. Together, they transform heterogeneous genomic resources into standardized capabilities that an LLM agent can combine for different clinical questions. Methodologically, we developed the skill library and system workflow through six stages: broad scanning of domain resources; LLM-assisted prioritization and expert selection; iterative skill development and testing; graph-based organization of related skills and their prerequisites; task-specific retrieval and progressive disclosure of skill instructions; and integration of multimodal inputs into an online interface. At inference, this organization enables the system to start from skills matched to a request, add their prerequisites and expose detailed instructions only when needed, limiting irrelevant context while preserving flexible workflows. This process converts established guidelines, databases and analytical tools into executable skills, while allowing ClinGeX to retrieve and compose only the capabilities required for each analysis (Fig. 1b).

To evaluate both the performance and clinical utility of ClinGeX, we conducted two independent studies. We assessed its autonomous analytical performance across 223 cases against OpenAI DeepResearch [18], representing a state-of-the-art commercial general-purpose research system, and Biomni [19], a leading open-source biomedical agent from academia. ClinGeX substantially outperformed both systems, achieving 71.7% concordance with expert consensus, 26.0 percentage points above the strongest comparator; moreover, 74.9% of its reports were judged directly adoptable without substantial revision by senior physicians, exceeding both comparators by more than 40 percentage points. More importantly, to determine whether these capabilities could translate into meaningful support for clinicians, we conducted a randomized multicentre study involving 45 clinical genomic professionals from three medical centres and 135 retrospectively collected real-world cases spanning criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease, and molecular oncology decision-making (Fig. 1c). DeepSeek11 1 Official website: https://chat.deepseek.com/ [20] was included as an accessible and representative example of widely used general-purpose LLM assistants. ClinGeX-assisted clinicians achieved significantly higher case-level concordance across all three scenarios, reaching 51.1%, 57.8%, and 64.4%, compared with 22.2%, 28.9%, and 31.1% for clinicians-only and 15.6%, 31.1%, and 20.0% with DeepSeek assistance. ClinGeX assistance also improved evidence identification and reduced the median time for criterion-level variant analysis from 60 to 15 minutes. Together, these findings support ClinGeX as a potential “Co-Clinician” [21, 22], augmenting rather than replacing expert genomic decision-making.

Finally, to preliminarily assess its utility in routine clinical-genomics work, we evaluated ClinGeX over a prespecified one-month period of routine use, during which 11 experienced clinical genomics professionals from multiple medical centers used the system for self-directed, naturally occurring tasks and provided structured feedback on 96 completed analyses (Fig. 1d). Experts reported fully or partially adopting ClinGeX’s conclusions in 94.8% of tasks, while time savings of more than 15 minutes were reported for 77.3% of difficult tasks. Together, these complementary evaluations support the potential of a skill-centred, domain-grounded agent to improve the accuracy, efficiency, and practical scalability of clinical genomic analysis.

2 Results

2.1 ClinGeX Overview

ClinGeX is an LLM-driven agent for clinical genomic analysis. Through a chatbot interface (Fig. 1a), users can submit free-text requests together with optional multimodal materials, including pedigree images, clinical records and other file types. The system returns a free-text reports accompanied by a concise summary of the analytical workflow, evidence sources and key intermediate outputs to support traceability.

At its core, ClinGeX uses a skill-centred architecture comprising 105 atomic clinical-genomics skills. For each request, a skill selector decomposes the task, retrieves relevant skills and expands the selection using semantic and prerequisite relationships encoded in a skill graph. The agent then executes the resulting task-specific workflow iteratively and synthesizes the accumulated evidence into its final response. Actions and tool outputs are retained in the execution record for review. Further details of the system architecture and development are provided in Methods Sec. 4.1.

We next evaluated ClinGeX across three settings of increasing clinical realism: automated system benchmarks, a controlled human–AI collaboration study, and prospective assessment in real-world clinical-genomics use. Together, these evaluations examined standalone performance, effects on clinician performance, and perceived utility in routine workflows.

2.2 System-level Analysis of ClinGeX on Automated Benchmarks

To evaluate ClinGeX at scale, we constructed a benchmark comprising 223 clinical-genomics cases released after the knowledge cutoff of the underlying model of the comparators, collected from five expert-curated resources: ClinVar [23] for SNV interpretation (n=79), ClinGen [24, 25] for gene–disease validity assessment (n=66), and CIViC [26, 27], OncoKB [28, 29] and PharmGKB [30] for clinical-actionability classification (n=78). The primary metric was final-answer concordance, defined as agreement with all required components of the reference standard. Shared secondary outcomes included repeat consistency and execution time. Task-specific outcomes assessed pathogenicity discrimination and evidence recovery for SNV interpretation; classification severity and genetic and experimental evidence coverage for gene–disease validity; and complete-answer accuracy and classification severity for clinical actionability. Exact definitions, denominators and scoring procedures are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.4. To assess potential leakage from the reference databases, we audited execution records for direct or indirect retrieval of source information and confirmed that no evaluated execution retrieved such information (Supplementary Table 6).

In Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Secs. A.5 and A.6, we conducted ablation studies to assess the contribution of the ClinGeX architecture and its robustness across different agent cores. Here, we used the final ClinGeX configuration with DeepSeek-V4 as the agent core and compared it with the domain-specialized OpenBioLLM [31] and the latest agents, DeepResearch (OpenAI) [18], SciSpace [32], Biomni [19] and TxAgent [33]. General-purpose LLMs such as GPT and DeepSeek were not benchmarked separately because they underlie the evaluated agents. Configurations are detailed in Supplementary Sec. A.4.2.

ClinGeX outperforms domain-specialized LLMs and agents across all three tasks.

ClinGeX achieved the highest final concordance in each task (Fig. 2a–c): 89.9% for SNV interpretation, 53.0% for gene–disease validity and 72.3% for clinical actionability. The corresponding best baseline results were 49.4% for DeepResearch, 35.5% for Biomni and 52.3% for TxAgent. Repeat consistency remained high across the three tasks (87.9–93.7%). Mean execution time was 175–197,s, broadly comparable to other agentic systems and shorter than SciSpace (496–727,s).

For SNV interpretation, ClinGeX achieved 100% sensitivity and 92.4% specificity for pathogenicity identification, with 82.3% weighted evidence recall, 84.8% evidence-strength concordance and a 1.3% significant-error rate. In gene–disease validity assessment, it reported usable genetic and experimental evidence scores for 90.9% of cases, compared with 28.8% and 15.2%, respectively, for the strongest comparator. For clinical-actionability classification, complete-answer accuracy was 57.7%, compared with 26.9% for TxAgent, while severe over- and under-classification remained infrequent.

ClinGeX produces higher-quality and more clinically usable reports in blinded expert review.

We additionally compared the free-text reports produced by ClinGeX, Biomni and DeepResearch with human rating, jointly considering the correctness of key results and the soundness of the reasoning. Within each task, cases were partitioned among three domain experts (nine experts in total), each of whom rated the three shuffled and de-identified system reports for their assigned cases. Reports were evaluated on three-level ordinal dimensions covering overall acceptability, required revision, citation accuracy, guideline adherence, evidence use and interpretation, fabricated content and potential clinical risk (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Sec. A.4.7).

The proportion of ClinGeX reports receiving the highest overall-acceptability rating was 88.6% for SNV interpretation, 66.7% for gene–disease validity and 67.9% for clinical actionability. The corresponding proportions were 32.9%, 40.9% and 23.1% for DeepResearch and 34.2%, 43.9% and 17.9% for Biomni. ClinGeX received higher ratings across all assessed dimensions in the first two tasks. In clinical-actionability classification, its clearest advantages were in overall acceptability, guideline adherence, evidence completeness and evidence interpretation, whereas citation accuracy and avoidance of fabrication were similar across systems. These findings suggest that the performance advantage of ClinGeX extends beyond final classification to the quality and usability of its supporting analysis.

ClinGeX can ground its classifications in guideline-consistent analysis.

To more directly illustrate its capability, we selected three cases in which ClinGeX matched the reference classification while Biomni and DeepResearch did not (Fig. 3). In a SNV interpretation case, ClinGeX weighted two complementary functional studies against a discordant computational prediction without over-crediting it, reaching Likely Pathogenic where both comparators reported Pathogenic. In another gene-disease validity case, it partitioned genetic and experimental support into explicit, separately scored criteria, supporting a Limited classification where Biomni and DeepResearch reported Moderate and Definitive, respectively. In a clinical actionability case, it distinguished short-term glucose-response from longer-term HbA1c endpoints and weighed replication across overlapping cohorts, reaching Level 3 where the comparators reported Level 2A and Level 2B. In each case, the figure traces the classification to specific, guideline-grounded analytical steps that the comparators omitted, together illustrating ClinGeX’s capacity for integrative synthesis of heterogeneous evidence and for discriminating among evidentiary sources of differing strength.

2.3 Evaluation of ClinGeX in the MRMC Human-AI Collaboration Study

We next conducted a three-centre, multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) study to assess whether ClinGeX could improve human performance in three clinical-genomics scenarios: criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making. Each scenario comprised 45 cases, yielding 135 cases in total. Fifteen clinical genomic professionals with 3–10 years of relevant experience participated in each scenario (45 participants overall), with one scenario evaluated at each of three centres: Xinhua Hospital; the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, CUHK; and Shanghai Chest Hospital. Participants completed cases under three conditions: human-only, DeepSeek-aided and ClinGeX-aided. DeepSeek was selected as an accessible and widely used general-purpose LLM comparator.

A Latin-square-inspired counterbalanced design minimized learning and order effects [34] (Extended Data Fig. 2). Each participant completed nine cases—three per condition—without encountering the same case twice. Each case was evaluated under all three conditions by three different participants, and condition order was randomized across participants. Further details are provided in Methods Sec. 4.2.

ClinGeX assistance is associated with higher case-level concordance.

We first assessed whether ClinGeX could improve participants’ final-answer correctness. We used case-level concordance as the primary metric, defined as the proportion of assessments for which the participant’s final conclusion was adjudicated by the expert panel as substantially correct (Supplementary Sec. A.7.2). ClinGeX assistance produced the highest concordance in all three scenarios (Fig. 4a). For criterion-level variant analysis, observed concordance was 51.1%, compared with 22.2% under human-only assessment and 15.6% with DeepSeek assistance; the corresponding GLMM-standardized differences were 29.9 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=0.013P=0.013) and 36.8 points (P=0.009P=0.009), respectively. For genomic interpretation in rare disease, observed concordance was 57.8%, compared with 28.9% and 31.1%, respectively; the GLMM-standardized differences were 29.6 points (P=0.017P=0.017) and 27.3 points (P=0.019P=0.019). For molecular oncology decision-making, observed concordance was 64.4%, compared with 31.1% and 20.0%, respectively; the GLMM-standardized differences were 33.4 points (P=0.002P=0.002) and 44.5 points (P<0.001P<0.001). Thus, under the current analysis, ClinGeX assistance approximately doubled concordance relative to routine and DeepSeek-aided assessment.

ClinGeX assistance improves key components of the supporting analysis.

We next evaluated task-specific intermediate outcomes, including evidence identification and weighting, phenotype interpretation and clinical-actionability assessment. Specifically, criterion-level variant analysis was evaluated using ACMG/AMP evidence recall, unsupported-evidence assignment, evidence-strength concordance, final-class accuracy and directional classification errors; genomic interpretation in rare disease using variant-classification and phenotype-interpretation accuracy and directional errors; and molecular oncology decision-making using panel-adjudicated free-response accuracy and the accuracy and directional errors of clinical-appropriateness judgements (Supplementary Sec. A.7.3).

In criterion-level variant analysis (Fig. 4b), ClinGeX increased model-standardized ACMG/AMP evidence recall by 28.6 (percentage) points relative to human-only assessment and by 27.9 points relative to DeepSeek assistance (both P<0.001P<0.001). It reduced unsupported evidence assignments by 10.4 (P=0.009P=0.009) and 15.3 points (P<0.001P<0.001), respectively, and improved evidence-strength concordance by 9.9 (P=0.015P=0.015) and 20.2 points (P<0.001P<0.001). Final pathogenicity-classification accuracy was 23.1 points higher than with DeepSeek assistance (P=0.040P=0.040), and over-classification was reduced by 9.2 and 11.1 points relative to human-only and DeepSeek-aided assessment, respectively (both P=0.034P=0.034); the remaining directional contrasts were not statistically significant.

In genomic interpretation in rare disease (Fig. 4c), model-standardized phenotype-interpretation accuracy increased by 23.7 (percentage) points relative to human-only assessment (P<0.001P<0.001), accompanied by a 12.8-point reduction in under-interpretation (P=0.006P=0.006). Accuracy was 8.8 points higher than with DeepSeek assistance, although this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.071P=0.071). Improvements in final classification were also numerical rather than statistically significant.

In molecular oncology decision-making (Fig. 4d), model-standardized free-response accuracy increased by 38.3 percentage points relative to DeepSeek assistance (P=0.001P=0.001) and by 22.2 points relative to human-only assessment (P=0.033P=0.033). Accuracy in judging the appropriateness of clinical decisions increased by 18.5 and 20.1 points relative to the human-only and DeepSeek-aided conditions, respectively (both P<0.001P<0.001); overestimation of appropriateness decreased by 15.1 (P=0.001P=0.001) and 16.8 points (P<0.001P<0.001), respectively. These findings suggest that the observed gains extended to several intermediate components of evidence assessment and clinical interpretation.

Confidence–correctness alignment is preserved with ClinGeX assistance.

In Fig. 5a, we examined whether improved concordance came at the cost of poorer uncertainty calibration. Certainty in criterion-level variant analysis was derived from whether participants made an explicit call for every applicable ACMG/AMP evidence item; the other two scenarios used self-reported confidence ratings. Metric definitions are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.7.4.

For criterion-level variant analysis, an assessment was counted as fully certain when the participant assigned an explicit call to every applicable ACMG/AMP evidence item, and as partially certain otherwise; accuracy within a group is the proportion of its assessments adjudicated concordant. Of the 45 assessments per condition, 9 were fully certain under ClinGeX assistance and 8 of these were correct (88.9%), against 21 of the remaining 36 (58.3%); the corresponding figures were 7 of 10 (70.0%) under DeepSeek assistance and 3 of 7 (42.9%) in the human-only condition. Certainty was thus most predictive of correctness under ClinGeX assistance, although the small number of fully certain assessments limits formal comparison.

For genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making, confidence–correctness alignment was assessed using point-biserial correlation, ROC–AUC and the Brier score. ClinGeX produced the highest correlation and lowest Brier score in both scenarios ((r=0.343), Brier score 0.246 for genomic interpretation in rare disease; (r=0.212), Brier score 0.161 for molecular oncology decision-making). It also produced the highest AUC in molecular oncology decision-making (0.652); its AUC in genomic interpretation in rare disease was 0.655, marginally below that of DeepSeek (0.671). Overall, the increase in concordance with ClinGeX was not accompanied by poorer confidence–correctness alignment.

Participants report a favorable experience and shorter completion times with ClinGeX.

Inspired by prior clinical AI evaluations [35], we also evaluated the system from readers’ perspective. Specifically, after completing the test, participants rated their experience with DeepSeek and with ClinGeX on an anonymous five-point Likert-type items covering confidence in the answers provided, willingness to use the system again, satisfaction with the presentation of results, smoothness of operation, and reliance on system output (Fig. 5b); ratings were summarized separately for each scenario, by the 15 participants who had completed it in the MRMC study (n=15n=15 per scenario, 45 in total). More details are in Methods Sec. 4.2.6. ClinGeX received higher mean ratings than DeepSeek on most dimensions in all three scenarios, the only exceptions being smoothness in genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (Fig. 5c).

We next compared self-reported mean time per question across the human-only, DeepSeek-aided and ClinGeX-aided conditions (Fig. 5d). Relative to human-only, ClinGeX shortened the median time per question from 60 to 15 min for criterion-level variant analysis and from 30 to 15 min for genomic interpretation in rare disease; both differences were statistically significant (P=0.003P=0.003 for both). For molecular oncology decision-making, the median time decreased from 15 to 11 min, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (P=0.078P=0.078). This smaller effect likely reflects the shorter human-only baseline in this task, together with the fact that participant-estimated times included system response latency.

As an exploratory analysis of spontaneous continued use, we recorded new conversations initiated in the two weeks following test completion, without any instruction or inducement for the 45 participants to continue using ClinGeX. Twenty-nine participants initiated at least one further conversation beyond the three study-related sessions, generating 239 new conversations in total, with a mean of 8.2 additional conversations per continuing user (Fig. 5e). These observations provide preliminary evidence of the system’s acceptability and voluntary reuse beyond the controlled study setting.

2.4 Prospective Assessment of ClinGeX on Real World Feedbacks

Controlled evaluations establish performance on standardized cases, but do not capture usability across heterogeneous, self-directed clinical-genomics tasks. We therefore conducted an exploratory, prospective task-based assessment in which experienced professionals submitted self-selected gene- and variant-interpretation tasks over a prespecified one-month period. “Prospective” refers to the forward collection of these evaluation tasks and participant feedback. This was a non-interventional, research-only evaluation, and ClinGeX outputs were not permitted to influence clinical reports, patient management or any other clinical decision.

Eleven senior clinical genomic professionals from five medical centres used ClinGeX in routine practice during a one-month period. The analysis here focused on clinicians’ episode-level feedback. An analysis episode was defined as one complete clinical-genomics objective—for example, interpreting a patient’s genomic sequencing findings or determining whether newly published evidence supported a specific variant- or gene–disease conclusion. An episode could comprise multiple dialogue turns, but its scope and analytical workflow were otherwise unrestricted. After completing an episode, the expert selected the corresponding conversation history and submitted one structured feedback record evaluating ClinGeX’s contribution to the episode as a whole, rather than to an individual prompt or turn. Thus, one feedback submission represented one completed episode; 96 submissions were collected. These records were then used to examine when and how ClinGeX helped in routine practice. For each episode, experts rated its difficulty (simple, moderate or difficult), indicated whether they adopted ClinGeX’s conclusion (fully, partially or not) and, where applicable, how many recommended evidence criteria they adopted, reported the time saved, and rated the help provided in information standardization, numerical analysis, literature analysis, and analytical or procedural guidance from little or no help to very helpful (Fig. 6a). Full definitions of these measures are in Methods Sec. 4.3.

Experts frequently rate ClinGeX conclusions as adoptable and report time savings.

We analysed the reported contribution of ClinGeX at two direct, episode-level endpoints: the extent to which its conclusion was adopted in the clinician’s final assessment and whether its use accelerated completion of the analysis. Across the 96 feedback records, experts rated the conclusion as fully adoptable in 70 episodes (72.9%), partially adopting it in 21 episodes (21.9%), and not adopting it in 5 episodes (5.2%) (Fig. 6b). They reported saving more than 15 min in 40 episodes (41.7%) and 5–15 min in another 50 episodes (52.1%); only 6 tasks (6.3%) took the same amount of time or longer. Full adoption was reported for 4/5 (80.0%) simple, 51/69 (73.9%) moderate and 15/22 (68.2%) difficult episodes. The corresponding proportions for which more than 15 min was saved were 0/5, 23/69 (33.3%) and 17/22 (77.3%), respectively, showing that the reported time benefit was concentrated in more difficult analyses while most final conclusions were fully adopted.

Experts adopt most of the evidence items recommended by ClinGeX.

As a more direct measure of assistance in routine variant interpretation, we identified 37 of the 96 feedback records that concerned variant-interpretation episodes for which ClinGeX recommended discrete ACMG/AMP evidence codes and the senior expert recorded how many were ultimately adopted. For each episode, we calculated the ratio of adopted to recommended codes, capped at 1. The mean adoption ratio was 0.83 for simple episodes (n=2n=2), 0.87 for moderate episodes (n=30n=30), and 0.80 for difficult episodes (n=5n=5) (Fig. 6c). Although the small numbers of simple and difficult episodes preclude comparisons between difficulty levels, these results show that experts retained a large proportion of the ACMG/AMP evidence codes proposed by ClinGeX in their final variant interpretations.

ClinGeX helps experts across multiple dimensions in analysis workflow.

Because ClinGeX was designed around five recurring operations in clinical genomics—guideline following, entity mapping, data-source lookup, numerical calculation and model-based prediction—we next examined the specific aspects of analysis in which clinicians found the system helpful. Experts separately rated its contribution to information standardization, numerical analysis, literature analysis, and analytical or procedural guidance. These four clinician-facing dimensions captured overlapping manifestations of the five skill categories: information standardization primarily reflected entity mapping and structured data retrieval; numerical analysis reflected numerical calculation and model-based prediction; literature analysis reflected data-source lookup; and analytical or procedural guidance reflected guideline following and cross-skill orchestration. Across the 96 episodes, mean helpfulness scores on a 0–2 scale were similar across the four dimensions, at 1.29, 1.35, 1.33 and 1.34, respectively (Fig. 6d). Some or substantial help was reported for 90 episodes (93.8%) in information standardization, 91 (94.8%) in numerical analysis, 89 (92.7%) in literature analysis, and 92 (95.8%) in analytical or procedural guidance. Thus, clinicians reported that ClinGeX supported multiple components of genomic interpretation rather than a single analytical function.

Case studies illustrate how ClinGeX contributes to clinical genomics analyses.

Two cases from the prospective deployment illustrate how ClinGeX helped clinicians address ambiguities with consequences for evidence use and clinical interpretation (Fig. 7). In an assessment of LRP6 c.1831C>>T (p.Arg611Cys), reported as moderately difficult by the submitting clinician, a ClinVar submission cited a family carrying p.Tyr418His as evidence for the assessed variant. ClinGeX identified this mismatch, helping the clinician avoid attributing that family’s evidence to p.Arg611Cys. The clinician reported full adoption of the conclusion, adoption of four of five recommended evidence criteria, and 5–15 min saved, and explicitly noted that the analysis helped avoid incorrect use of family evidence. In a second case, reported as difficult by the submitting clinician, TP53 c.391A>>T (p.Asn131Tyr) was detected at a variant allele fraction of 8–18% in blood from an old man with metastatic prostate cancer. The key question was whether this finding supported a hereditary cancer-risk interpretation. ClinGeX distinguished possible origins, including clonal haematopoiesis, tumour-derived DNA and constitutional mosaicism, separated germline and somatic interpretation frameworks, and proposed confirmation of sample type and additional tissue testing before assigning hereditary risk. The clinician reported full adoption of the conclusion and more than 15 min saved, highlighting the separate germline and somatic scenarios as particularly helpful.

3 DISCUSSION

Genomic analysis increasingly informs multiple stages of clinical care, from understanding disease mechanisms and establishing molecular diagnoses to guiding targeted interventions and population-level screening. Its broader adoption, however, is constrained by the specialized expertise required, uneven access to specialist support across centres and the difficulty of translating rapidly evolving knowledge into clinical practice. Contemporary artificial intelligence, particularly large language model (LLM)-based agentic systems, has shown promise in supporting clinical decision-making across several medical settings. Realizing this potential in clinical genomics requires systems that can reliably integrate fragmented and continuously evolving guidelines, massive databases and computational tools. Yet most evaluations remain benchmark- or simulation-based, leaving limited evidence of their effects on clinician performance and usability in workflow-relevant settings.

The central contribution of this work is ClinGeX, a skill-centred agent that adapts general-purpose LLMs into clinically grounded assistants for genomic analysis. Its technical value lies in three respects. First, systematic resource collection and expert curation help reduce the omissions and selection biases associated with ad hoc resource enumeration, and may offer a template for analogous skill discovery in other clinical domains. Second, semi-automated skill construction and graph-based organization allow the skill library to expand without sacrificing efficient task-specific retrieval. Third, progressive disclosure restricts the active context to what each analytical step requires, helping constrain hallucination. The value of these design choices is supported by the automated benchmark, in which the resulting system outperformed both alternative enhancement strategies and SOTA general-purpose and biomedical agents.

Across the automated benchmarks, human–AI collaboration study, and prospective deployment, we demonstrate the potential practical value of ClinGeX in five complementary aspects. First, it constrains the hallucination that current LLM-based systems cannot reliably avoid, grounding conclusions in executed skills and the evidence they return; the risk this addresses is visible in the DeepSeek-aided arm, where concordance fell below that of unassisted clinicians in two of the three scenarios (15.6% versus 22.2%; 20.0% versus 31.1%). Second, it improves the quality of gene-related clinical analysis and decision-making by junior and middle-grade clinicians, raising case-level concordance with expert consensus from 22.2%, 28.9% and 31.1% to 51.1%, 57.8% and 64.4% across the three scenarios—a meaningful step towards democratizing access to expert-level interpretation. Third, it lowers interpretive burden, shortening the median time per case from 60 to 15 min for criterion-level variant analysis and from 30 to 15 min for genomic interpretation in rare disease, while presenting the complete interpretive path so that clinicians can inspect it and decide whether to adopt or override the system’s conclusion. Fourth, it showed broad workflow-level utility for experienced clinical-genomics professionals during self-directed routine use, as reflected by reported benefits spanning information retrieval and standardization, numerical and literature analysis, and procedural guidance. Fifth, the system can be deployed locally and adapts to a range of open- and closed-source backbone models, which accommodates the differing infrastructural constraints and access policies of individual medical centres.

Limitations

First of all, although ClinGeX targets clinical genomic analysis broadly, the MRMC study covered only three scenarios—criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making—selected based on the participating centres’ specialties and routine caseloads. Although the skill library was not tuned to these scenarios, their evaluation does not establish generalizability to other areas of clinical genomic interpretation, such as polygenic risk assessment.

Secondly, the MRMC study was powered to detect the main effect of assistance; with 45 readers and 135 cases, several secondary comparisons showed consistent directions but did not all reach statistical significance. The primary endpoint is a proxy: concordance with expert consensus reflects interpretive quality rather than patient outcomes. Although fit for the present aim of assessing interpretive performance, establishing that improved interpretation translates into changes in clinical management and supports broader clinical use will require a prospective randomized trial with prespecified clinical endpoints.

Finally, the prospective deployment focused on workflow-level outcomes—including conclusion adoption, time savings and perceived helpfulness—rather than prespecified clinical endpoints such as diagnostic yield, changes in management or patient outcomes. It therefore provides evidence of practical utility in routine analysis, while the downstream clinical impact of ClinGeX requires evaluation in larger prospective studies.

4 METHODS

4.1 Development of ClinGeX

ClinGeX adopts a skill-centred agentic architecture. An agent ‘skill’ [36] is a reusable instruction module, written in structured free text, that encapsulates a task-specific agentic workflow for a particular clinical or research task. Each skill specifies when it should be invoked and provides the procedural knowledge required to complete the task, including what information to seek, which standards and resources to consult, which tools to call, and how to carry out the analysis step by step (a detailed description on skills can be found in Supplementary Sec. A.2.1). By defining these capabilities at an atomic level, a broad and systematically curated skill library allows the agent to flexibly select, combine, and sequence individual skills to construct task-specific workflows, thereby supporting a wide range of clinical genomic analysis needs.

To build the skill library and integrate it into an LLM-based agent, we developed ClinGeX through a six-stage design framework. Stages 1–4 focused on constructing the skill library by identifying, curating, and formalizing domain knowledge and analytical resources into atomic agent skills. Stage 5 integrated these skills into the agent workflow through inference-time skill retrieval and orchestration, while Stage 6 focused on user interface and interaction design.

Stage 1. Web-scale scan of domain resources.

To systematically build the skill library, we first conducted a web-scale scan to identify and collect a broad range of clinical-genomics resources for subsequent skill construction. Specifically, we organized the scan into five broad categories of clinical-genomic analysis operations: guideline following, entity mapping, data-source lookup, numerical calculation, and model-based prediction. Together, these categories capture common needs in genomic analysis, including applying clinical guidelines, converting heterogeneous entity identifiers, querying case- or cohort-level evidence from genomic and clinical databases, performing standardized calculations, and predicting the functional effects of genomic variants.

Because resources in these five categories are organized differently across the web, we did not use a shared search strategy for all categories. Instead, for each category, we first selected an existing broad-coverage collection as the primary source for automated resource extraction, and then manually added other important resources that were not captured. For example, to identify resources for data-source lookup, we extracted all 2,594 database entries from the cumulative alphabetical index of the Nucleic Acids Research Database Issue rather than searching it with a limited set of keywords. Because no single catalogue covers the full range of resources used in clinical genomics, we supplemented these entries with records from bio.tools, re3data.org and FAIRsharing.org and then merged records that referred to the same resource. The other four groups were scanned using the same general principle but with sources suited to each type of resource; the complete sources, search procedures and coverage limits are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.2.2 and all considered websites are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

This stage yielded 195 guidelines, 3,508 entity-mapping tools and services, 41,000 databases and resources for evidence lookup, 53 reproducible calculation methods, and 144 prediction models, forming the initial pool of candidate resources for agent skill construction. Notably, each candidate was represented by its associated free-text documentation; for example, tools, databases, and models were represented by their ‘README’ files, documentation pages, model cards, or related methodological descriptions.

Stage 2. LLM-assisted resource filtering and expert review.

To further improve the quality of the candidate resources identified in Stage 1, we filtered them in Stage 2 based on their clinical relevance, reliability, and suitability for skill construction. We adopted an LLM–human hybrid filtering pipeline, in which an LLM first evaluated the candidate resources using category-specific criteria, followed by final review and selection by clinical experts.

Similar as Stage 1, the LLM rating pipeline was tailored to each resource category. For each category, we predefined a set of evaluation rubrics and prompted the LLM to assess each candidate against each rubric separately. For the entity mapping, data-source lookup, numerical calculation, and model-based prediction categories, the rubrics were quantitative, with the LLM assigning a numerical score to each rubric (e.g., 0–5). These rubric-level scores were then combined as a weighted sum to produce an overall score from 0 to 100. Based on this score, candidates were assigned to Tier 1 (≥75\geq 75), Tier 2 (55–74), Tier 3 (35–54), or exclusion (<35<35), with higher-tier candidates prioritized for subsequent review. In contrast, guideline-following candidates were assessed qualitatively: the LLM provided detailed comments on each predefined rubric without assigning numerical scores or tier levels. We designed this mainly because guidelines are typically high-value resources that warrant careful consideration. Providing a single numerical score or tier could lead subsequent reviewers to rely on that summary judgment. We therefore retained free-text comments, requiring experts to examine the underlying rationale and reach more considered conclusions. In general, the rubrics focused on the authority, currency, verifiability, and accessibility of guidelines; the clinical relevance, reliability, and accessibility of data and mapping resources; and the reproducibility, clinical support, and practical deployability of computational methods and predictive models. The complete rubrics, scoring instructions, and weights for each operation type are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

Eight clinical experts from seven institutions then reviewed the candidates for clinical utility, technical reliability, and functional redundancy, with the LLM-generated assessments provided as supporting material. Importantly, the LLM-derived tiers were used only to prioritize candidates for expert review and did not serve as strict inclusion thresholds. Final inclusion was determined by consensus among the eight clinicians, and lower-tier candidates could still be retained if they addressed important clinical needs not adequately covered by higher-ranked resources. More details are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.2.3.

After filtering, 105 candidate resource documents remained for skill construction: 27 for guideline following, 13 for entity mapping, 30 for data-source lookup, 12 for numerical calculation, and 23 for model-based prediction.

Stage 3. Skill curation through recursive optimization.

In this stage, we translated the 105 selected resources into standardized, executable agent skills and iteratively refined them through a builder–evaluator loop inspired by recursive self-improvement [37, 38]. We first consolidated the five resource categories described above into three functional skill classes: guide, search, and analysis. Guide skills were derived from clinical guidelines and other normative documents; search skills from resources for entity mapping and data-source lookup, including databases, search services, and their APIs; and analysis skills from numerical methods and predictive machine-learning models.

Each skill was initially compiled by a ‘builder’ agent based on DeepSeek-V4. The builder received the corresponding source materials together with a class-specific construction prompt and generated an initial skill implementation. For guide skills, it translated source documents into stepwise procedures and traceable decision rules. For search skills, it specified how to query the target resource, including accepted inputs, query procedures, and processing of returned records. For analysis skills, it implemented the required calculations or specified how predictive models should be invoked and their outputs interpreted. Across all three classes, each skill was represented by a standardized SKILL.md file defining its scope, inputs, execution workflow, outputs, and limitations, accompanied, where necessary, by executable scripts and supporting references. The complete construction prompts and skill specification are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.2.4.

To verify and iteratively improve each compiled skill, we employed a separate ‘evaluator’ agent. Based on the source materials and the initial skill implementation, the evaluator automatically generated 5–20 skill-specific test cases, each specifying an input, the expected action or procedure, and the expected output or behaviour (representative examples are provided in Supplementary Table 3). The resulting test cases were then executed by a separate execution agent, instantiated as an LLM equipped with the corresponding skill. For each failed case, the evaluator summarized the observed failure in free text and provided the corresponding test output to the builder. The builder then revised the relevant skill instructions, interface specification, or executable code as appropriate, and the updated skill was subsequently re-evaluated using the same procedure. This builder–evaluation–revision cycle continued until all identified failures were resolved or a maximum of five revision cycles was reached, resulting in 105 agent skills. The workflow is illustrated in Extended Data Fig. 4.

Stage 4. Graph construction for scalable skill organization.

After obtaining the final 105 skills, we organized them into a skill graph to support more efficient skill retrieval and combination. In the graph, each skill was represented as a node, and we exhaustively considered all possible pairwise relationships among the 105 skills, yielding (1052)=5,460\binom{105}{2}=5,460 unordered skill pairs. Each pair was then evaluated for two types of relationships: functional relatedness and prerequisite dependence. For each skill pair, an LLM first assessed functional relatedness along five dimensions—purpose similarity, input overlap, substitutability, complementarity, and joint use—assigning each a score from 0 to 4. These scores were summed to form an undirected relatedness edge weight ranging from 0 to 20. Separately, a directed prerequisite edge was added when one skill required another to obtain or interpret its output. The resulting graph contained 28 directed prerequisite edges. Relatedness weights support the retrieval of complementary skills, whereas prerequisite edges preserve required workflow steps. New skills can be incorporated by evaluating only their relationships with existing nodes. Further details are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.3.

Stage 5. Context management based on progressive disclosure.

Till here, Stages 1–4 established the core of ClinGeX: a skill library organized as a skill graph. During inference, this graph is integrated into the host LLM’s context through task-specific retrieval and progressive plan–execute orchestration.

Given a task query, ClinGeX first invokes an LLM-based intent-recognition agent (Extended Data Fig. 5). The agent decomposes the user’s request into one to three concrete analytical needs. Each need is encoded using Qwen text-embedding-v4 [39], and cosine similarity is computed against the purpose and applicability descriptions of all 105 skills. The 30 highest-ranked skills form the seed set. For each seed, one-hop related skills with an edge weight of R≥8R\geq 8 are considered, and at most 15 additional skills are retained across all seeds. Three general literature- and web-search skills are included by default, after which prerequisite dependencies are recursively added until closure.

After retrieval, ClinGeX invokes a host agent that loads concise descriptions of all selected skills, each summarizing the skill’s capabilities, usage boundaries, and routing rules, and uses them to formulate an overall workflow plan. The host agent then instantiates sub-agents for individual workflow steps, each of which loads the complete instructions of the corresponding skill into its context and executes the assigned task according to the skill-specific workflow. More details of this stage are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.3.3.

Stage 6. Multimodal support and online deployment.

In the final stage, we implemented ClinGeX as a multimodal online system. Uploaded files were processed in parallel according to type. PDFs were directly converted into Markdown-formatted text using MinerU [40], whereas images, such as pedigree charts, were passed to Qwen3-VL [41] with a fixed instruction to generate descriptive summaries. The resulting texts were concatenated with the user’s query to form the input context.

We deployed ClinGeX as a web application supporting multiple backbone models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemini, GLM, GPT, Kimi, etc.), heterogeneous file uploads, and concurrent queries. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 3, the interface contains four components: a dialogue module for user input and file submission, an execution module that streams intermediate operations and tool results, a result module that presents the final structured analysis, and a user-management module for reviewing previous sessions and conducting follow-up analyses.

4.2 Conduct of the MRMC Human-AI Collaboration Study

We conducted a randomized, three-condition human–AI collaboration study following established MRMC design principles [42], with condition order and case-set assignment counterbalanced using a Latin-square-like allocation [43], and administered the study through an online evaluation platform (Supplementary Sec. A.7.1).

4.2.1 Task Scenarios

We evaluated ClinGeX in three clinical genomic analysis scenarios, selected to cover criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease, and molecular oncology decision-making, detailed as:

  • •

    ACMG-based variant pathogenicity classification and analysis (criterion-level variant analysis) Participants evaluated the applicability and evidence strength of each of the 28 ACMG/AMP criteria for a given variant and assigned a final pathogenicity classification. They also provided a written justification for their assessment, along with a confidence rating and the time taken to complete the task. This scenario primarily assessed participants’ ability to evaluate pathogenicity evidence according to the ACMG/AMP framework and integrate the applicable criteria into a final variant classification.

  • •

    Genomic interpretation in rare disease through integrated variant and phenotype assessment (genomic interpretation in rare disease). Participants evaluated whether the candidate genes and variants could explain the patient’s phenotype, integrating variant-level evidence with phenotype concordance and inheritance information. They provided an integrated case-level interpretation, together with a written justification, confidence rating, and completion time. This scenario primarily assessed participants’ ability to synthesize genetic and phenotypic evidence to determine the extent to which a candidate finding explained the patient’s disease.

  • •

    Molecular tumor analysis and action recommendation (molecular oncology decision-making). Participants reviewed the clinical and molecular information for a tumour case, proposed the most appropriate next analytical or clinical action, and evaluated the plausibility of a series of case-specific statements. They also reported their confidence and completion time. This scenario assessed the integration of molecular findings with clinical context, the identification of actionable evidence, and the distinction between supported and unsupported clinical recommendations.

Representative cases and complete task examples are provided in Supplementary Sec. A.7.6.

4.2.2 Tested Conditions

Each participant completed tasks under the following three assistance conditions:

  • •

    Routine condition. Participants completed the assigned tasks according to their routine clinical practice. They were allowed to access the internet and freely consult any literature, databases, or online resources that they would normally use in their routine workflow, but were not permitted to use any AI-based tools.

  • •

    DeepSeek-assisted condition. Participants had access to the same resources permitted in the unassisted condition and could additionally use DeepSeek through its official web interface.

  • •

    ClinGeX-assisted condition. Participants had access to the same resources permitted in the unassisted condition and could additionally use the deployed ClinGeX platform.

The assigned system was the only AI tool permitted in each assisted condition, and all other study procedures were kept consistent across conditions.

4.2.3 Data Preparation

In this section, we describe the evaluation data preparation procedures for the three clinical scenarios. For each scenario, we prepared 45 evaluation cases, resulting in a total of 135 cases:

  • •

    Criterion-level variant analysis. Five experienced genetic analysts from Xinhua Hospital, each routinely interpreting more than 500 variants per year in clinical practice, contributed 39 patient records involving 45 clinically validated variants. After de-identification, the patient phenotypes, target variants, and supporting literature used in the original clinical interpretation were assembled into 45 evaluation cases.

  • •

    Genomic interpretation in rare disease. We obtained 25 de-identified patients with rare diseases from the 2023-2025 curated laboratory quality control cases. An expert panel from CUHK carefully reviewed the clinical information, validated variants, interpretation reports, and corresponding VCF files. Additional clinically reportable variants, including secondary findings and candidate variants with partial phenotypic correlation, were selected from the VCF files and combined with the validated diagnostic variants, producing 45 evaluation cases with distinct candidate-variant sets. Different cases derived from the same original case were not assigned to the same participant.

  • •

    Molecular oncology decision-making. We retrieved 323 human molecular-oncology case reports published after 2025 from PubMed, comprising 186 digestive-system and 137 thoracic-tumour reports. The reports were processed using a multi-model question-generation and quality-control procedure, with details provided in the Supplementary Sec. A.7.7. Following expert review, 27 digestive-system and 18 thoracic-tumour cases were retained, yielding 45 evaluation cases. The selected cases were manually de-identified, and nonessential clinical details were redacted or reformulated to prevent AI systems from directly locating the corresponding source publications.

The research use of these clinical data was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xinhua Hospital.

4.2.4 Participant Recruitment

We enrolled 54 clinical genomic professionals as participants, comprising 45 readers and 9 adjudicators. For each of the three clinical scenarios, 15 readers with relevant domain expertise were recruited. The criterion-level variant analysis cohort consisted of genetic analysts with 3–8 years of experience, recruited through Xinhua Hospital and including analysts from other hospitals undertaking advanced clinical training there. The interpretation working group of genomic interpretation in rare disease comprised clinical geneticists, genomic laboratory analysts, and postdoctoral fellows with 3–10 years of experience from Hong Kong, Guangzhou, and Shandong, recruited through the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, The Chinese University of Hong Kong. For molecular oncology decision-making, 15 clinicians and resident trainees with approximately 4–10 years of clinical experience were recruited through Shanghai Chest Hospital, including 6 specializing in thoracic oncology and 9 in digestive-system oncology. A three-member expert adjudication panel was additionally recruited from each of the three centres for its corresponding clinical scenario; each panel comprised one senior clinician with over 10 years of experience and two additional members from the same department with over 5 years of experience. All participants gave informed consent for their study responses to be used for research analysis.

4.2.5 Study Procedure

Within each clinical scenario, the 45 cases were distributed among 15 readers using a Latin-square-like allocation scheme. Each reader completed nine cases: three in the unassisted condition, three in the DeepSeek-assisted condition, and three in the ClinGeX-assisted condition. The cases assigned to an individual reader did not overlap across conditions. Consequently, each of the 45 cases was evaluated three times, once under each condition and by a different reader. The order of the three conditions was randomized across readers. For each assigned case, participants reviewed the case description and accompanying materials, completed the scenario-specific assessment, and submitted their final conclusion, written justification, confidence rating, and completion time through the online evaluation platform.

Several measures were used to reduce potential learning, order, fatigue, and information-leakage effects. No reader encountered the same case more than once, and the balanced allocation prevented individual cases from being evaluated exclusively under a particular assistance condition. Participants were required to work independently, to refrain from using any AI tools other than those explicitly permitted under their assigned condition, and to avoid any attempt to identify the source or reference answer of a task. To limit fatigue, the nine cases were completed over a two-week period, and participants were asked to distribute them as evenly as possible across this period. During the study, the expert panel corresponding to each clinical scenario answered procedural questions without providing case-specific guidance. After all assessments had been completed, participant responses were evaluated according to the predefined primary and secondary outcomes. Outcomes requiring clinical judgement were assessed by the corresponding expert panels whereas objective outcomes were calculated from the submitted responses and recorded task data using prespecified criteria (Supplementary Sec. A.7.2, A.7.3).

4.2.6 Participant Post-study Survey

After completing all assigned tasks, the 45 readers completed the same anonymous post-study survey, with 15 readers for each clinical scenario. Participants were instructed to complete the survey independently based on their experience with the three study conditions. Survey responses were collected anonymously and de-identified before analysis.

The survey comprised 13 experience-related items. Three open-response items asked participants to estimate their average time per case under the routine, DeepSeek-assisted, and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. These estimates were used for the main time comparison because readers were not required to complete cases in a single uninterrupted session; platform timestamps could therefore include pauses or unrelated clinical work and were not treated as active analysis time. The remaining ten items assessed DeepSeek and ClinGeX separately across five clinician-reported dimensions using the following five-point ordinal scales:

  • •

    Confidence after assistance: substantially less confident than when working independently; somewhat disrupted by the system; about the same as when working independently; slightly more confident; or markedly more confident.

  • •

    Willingness to use the system again in clinical work: very unwilling; somewhat unwilling; neutral; somewhat willing; or very willing.

  • •

    Satisfaction with the presentation of results in a clinical context: very dissatisfied; somewhat dissatisfied; neutral; somewhat satisfied; or very satisfied.

  • •

    Smoothness of system operation: not at all smooth; not very smooth; moderately smooth; relatively smooth; or very smooth.

  • •

    Reliance on system output when completing the tasks: almost no reliance; reliance on a small part of the output; reliance on approximately half of the output; reliance on most of the output; or complete reliance.

4.3 Prospective, Non-interventional Feedback Collection of ClinGeX

Following the retrospective MRMC evaluation on controlled cases, we conducted an exploratory prospective task-based assessment to evaluate ClinGeX’s utility in daily clinical-genomics analysis, inspired by prior evaluations of clinical AI in real-world care [44, 45]. Here, “prospective” denotes the forward collection of participants’ routine clinical or research-level analysis tasks that were comparable in nature to the evaluation tasks. Experienced clinical professionals evaluated ClinGeX on tasks arising from their usual genomic-analysis work and provided structured feedback after completing each task. The system outputs were used solely for research evaluation and were not permitted to inform or alter clinical reports, patient management or any other clinical decision. To capture clinicians’ real-world needs and patterns of use, we did not prescribe a fixed set of cases or tasks, nor did we include a control condition. Accordingly, this study was intended to characterize the task-level utility of our system in a workflow-relevant, non-interventional setting.

4.3.1 Study Design and Participant Recruitment

We recruited 11 professionals engaged in clinical variant interpretation, each with more than five years of variant-interpretation experience and responsibility for preparing clinical reports for more than 500 cases per year. Six participants were from the Department of Genetics, Xinhua Hospital; two were from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, The Chinese University of Hong Kong; and one participant each was from the Department of Medical Genetics, Shandong Provincial Hospital, Anhui Provincial Hospital, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. None had participated in the preceding MRMC study.

Professionals used ClinGeX during their routine work over a prespecified one-month period. They were asked to submit feedback on clinical genomic analysis episodes for which they had actually used ClinGeX, including, but not limited to, variant interpretation, evidence retrieval, literature analysis, and case-level analysis. They were explicitly instructed to report their experience objectively, irrespective of whether ClinGeX had been beneficial, neutral, or detrimental to completion of the analysis. All of them gave informed consent for their submitted feedback to be used for research analysis.

4.3.2 Feedback Platform and Unit of Evaluation

We developed a platform to collect structured feedback on participants’ routine use of ClinGeX. The platform did not request or extract patient names, identifiers, clinical records, genomic data or other patient-level information. Participants were instructed to follow data-protection policies throughout their use of ClinGeX and submission of feedback, including avoiding the disclosure of potential identifiable patient information.

One feedback submission represented one completed real-world clinical-genomics analysis episode and assessed the contribution of ClinGeX across that episode as a whole. An episode could involve multiple rounds of interaction with ClinGeX; the selected conversation record was used only to associate the feedback with the corresponding episode and analysis process, rather than to define an individual message or dialogue turn as an independent evaluation. A post hoc comparison with platform conversation counts indicated feedback coverage of at least 86.5%, providing some reassurance against selective reporting (Supplementary Table 21).

4.3.3 Feedback Measures

The feedback measures were designed by a senior clinical-genomics physician at Xinhua Hospital with reference to a previous prospective clinical AI deployment study [46]. Each submission collected the following items:

  • •

    Analysis difficulty: simple, not requiring AI; moderate, for which AI could provide some assistance; or difficult, for which AI could provide substantial assistance.

  • •

    Adoption of ClinGeX’s conclusion: fully adopted; partially adopted; or not adopted. For variant-assessment episodes, adoption referred to whether and to what extent the participant retained ClinGeX’s proposed final pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance, likely benign or benign (P/LP/VUS/LB/B) classification in their final assessment. For other episodes, adoption referred to the principal task conclusion.

  • •

    Adoption of recommended evidence criteria: the number of evidence criteria recommended by ClinGeX and the number ultimately adopted by the participant. This item was optional and intended for episodes in which discrete evidence criteria were applicable.

  • •

    Time saved with ClinGeX: more than 15 min saved; 5–15 min saved; or no change in completion time or slower completion.

  • •

    Help with information standardization: very helpful or prevented an error; provided some help and saved time; or provided little or no help.

  • •

    Help with numerical analysis: very helpful and gave numerical retrieving or analysis that the participant might otherwise have missed; provided some help and saved time; or provided little or no help.

  • •

    Help with literature analysis: very helpful, identifying relevant literature and providing accurate interpretation; provided some useful interpretation; or provided little or no help.

  • •

    Help with analytical or procedural guidance: very helpful and provided a distinct, useful analytical approach; provided some help through a reasonably accurate routine analysis; or provided little or no help.

  • •

    Specific contribution to the episode: an optional free-text description of the assistance provided by ClinGeX.

All categorical items were required, whereas the evidence-criterion counts and free-text description were optional. Each submission was stored together with the participant identifier and selected conversation identifier.

5 Data availability

The data supporting the findings of this study are available upon reasonable request. Requests for data access should be directed to three-world@sjtu.edu.cn or to any of the corresponding-author email addresses.

6 Code availability

Although the source code for ClinGeX is not publicly available at present, an online deployed Chinese–English bilingual version of the system is available at https://chatgeno.internal.onexai.com.cn/ after registration.
