7 Extended Data

Appendix A Supplementary

A.1 Main System Prompt of ClinGeX

The following reproduces the complete content of the deployed top-level ClinGeX/SKILL.md, with line wrapping, dash characters and the directory-tree glyphs normalized only for typesetting. It makes the operating stance, routing order, progressive-disclosure policy and path-resolution rules auditable.

A.2 Details of Constructing the ClinGeX Skill Library

A.2.1 Skill Introduction

Each Agent Skill is a version-controlled directory organized as shown below. Lightweight metadata in SKILL.md supports discovery, while full instructions and optional resources are loaded only after selection. In ClinGeX, a skill represents a recurrent clinical-genomics operation and specifies the workflow and evidence needed to execute and interpret it safely.

Canonical Skill Directory <skill-name>/|-- SKILL.md required instructions and metadata|-- scripts/ optional executable actions and tests|-- references/ optional detailed source material‘-- assets/ optional templates and static data

Within this system-specific formulation, we retained two complementary taxonomies. The five construction action types—guideline following, entity mapping, data-source lookup, numerical calculation and model-based prediction—describe the clinical operation from which a prototype was discovered. The three deployment classes—guide, search and analysis—describe how the compiled skill is exposed at run time. The axes therefore need not coincide. For example, vep, mutalyzer3 and variant-validator were discovered as entity-mapping capabilities but are deployed under analysis because they perform executable transformations; conversely, ontology and identifier-mapping services are deployed under search. This mapping recovers the 27/13/30/12/23 construction counts reported in the main Methods while preserving the deployed 27/40/38 guide/search/analysis directory counts.

A.2.2 Resource Discovery across the Five Capability Categories

Discovery was frozen on 28–30 July 2026 and performed separately for the five action types (Supplementary Table 1). A raw source record, normalized candidate and retained skill prototype were distinct units; records could be merged or one document family could support multiple operations, so successive counts are not simple retention rates.

Category boundaries followed the primary operation: representational conversion was entity mapping, evidence retrieval was data-source lookup, reproducible formulas or decision rules were numerical calculation, and learned outputs were model-based prediction. Conservative record linkage favoured residual duplication over false merging, and the predictor landscape was missense-enriched rather than complete across variant classes.

A.2.3 Category-Specific LLM Triage and Expert Selection

LLMs were used to structure and prioritize the candidate space, not to make the final inclusion decision. Criterion scores were returned through structured schemas and combined deterministically using the weights in Supplementary Table 2. Numerical screens used the same prespecified tiers: Tier 1, ≥75\geq 75; Tier 2, 55–74; Tier 3, 35–54; and exclusion, <35<35. Scores supported ranking within an action type and were not compared across action types.

Maintenance and citation or adoption could not always be established from static catalogue metadata and were flagged for live verification rather than inferred. For data-source-lookup candidates, a score of zero for domain centrality, guideline recognition or programmatic access forced a one-tier downgrade. Guideline documents, calculations and predictors were not forced into the database rubric because database accessibility is not an appropriate proxy for normative authority, mathematical reproducibility or clinical calibration.

Eight clinical and domain experts from seven institutions reviewed the prioritized candidates: Xinhua Hospital; the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Faculty of Medicine, The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital; Shanghai Sixth People’s Hospital; Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center; Shanghai Chest Hospital; and Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine. Reviewers considered clinical utility, compatibility with authoritative standards, complementarity, unmet need, legitimacy and stability of access, documentation, technical reliability and functional redundancy. They could retain a lower-tier candidate that filled an uncovered clinical operation, remove a higher-tier but redundant or non-invocable candidate, or consolidate several candidates into one prototype. This process froze 105 prototypes: 27 guideline-following, 13 entity-mapping, 30 data-source-lookup, 12 numerical-calculation and 23 model-based-prediction skills.

The scan was a frozen, structured landscape survey rather than a preregistered systematic review. Coverage differed across action types, conservative record linkage could retain residual duplicates, and most LLM triage scores were not independently repeated. These limitations constrain claims of landscape completeness but do not alter the identity or counts of the final frozen prototypes.

A.2.4 Details of Skill Initialization and Iterative Optimization

Each operation retained after expert review was initialized as a self-contained skill by a builder agent. The builder was required to examine how the underlying guideline, database, tool, calculation or predictive model could be used across clinical-genomics workflows before defining the skill contract. The common initialization prompt is shown below; source documents, technical documentation and the intended operation were supplied with the prompt for each skill.

Prompt used to initialize a ClinGeX skill You are responsible for converting the supplied clinical-genomics resource or operation into a reliable, reusable agent skill. Study the source material and technical documentation before writing any files. Do not merely summarize the resource. Determine how it may be used in clinical practice and encode the procedures needed to use it correctly. 1. Characterize the resource. Establish its authoritative or evidentiary status, intended users, supported clinical domains and variant or data types, access method, version or update status, and any licence or authentication constraints. Distinguish normative rules, source assertions, deterministic calculations and model-derived predictions. 2. Enumerate applicable use cases. Consider all clinically plausible uses supported by the source, including direct lookup or calculation, interpretation of returned evidence, batch use, integration with upstream normalization and downstream classification, and use in incomplete or conflicting-evidence settings. Do not invent applications that are not supported by the source. 3. Define boundaries and dependencies. State when the skill should and should not be used, the required inputs and accepted representations, applicability restrictions, prerequisites, expected outputs, uncertainty, known limitations and failure conditions. Identify any guideline or companion skill required to interpret the result safely. 4. Construct the skill package. Create a directory containing a required SKILL.md and, where needed, scripts/, references/ and assets/. The SKILL.md must include valid front matter, concise discovery metadata, scope, use-when and do-not-use conditions, supported actions, required and optional inputs, a stepwise workflow, output interpretation, provenance requirements, limitations, error handling and brief examples. Place long criteria, source excerpts or lookup tables in references/; place reusable templates or static data in assets/. 5. Implement executable actions where appropriate. Scripts must use documented interfaces or reproducible published algorithms, validate inputs, preserve source provenance, return structured outputs, distinguish not_found from not_applicable and execution failure, support batch inputs where clinically useful, and never fabricate a result when an external service or required field is unavailable. 6. Prepare verification cases. Define tests before revision that collectively cover every exposed action, representative valid inputs, boundary values, alternative input representations, batch and multi-record responses, non-applicable cases, absent records, malformed inputs and anticipated external-service failures. For each test, specify the input, expected output fields or behaviour and an explicit pass criterion. Return the complete directory structure and file contents. Ensure that every claimed capability is supported by the supplied source, exposed through the documented interface and testable through the proposed verification cases.

Depending on the resource, initialization produced procedural instructions alone or combined them with executable scripts, indexed references and static assets. A separate test agent then received the compiled SKILL.md and ran 5–20 predefined cases through the same action interface used at run time. Failed cases triggered revision of the instructions, interface, implementation or limitation statement followed by rerunning the complete suite; iteration stopped when no actionable failure remained or after five cycles.

Supplementary Table 3 shows the complete verification suite for one representative analysis skill, REVEL. The suite was selected because it jointly tests external retrieval, variant applicability, alternative coordinate systems, multi-allelic and batch handling, missing results and clinically calibrated interpretation.

A.3 Details of Building the ClinGeX Skill Graph

A.3.1 Semantic Representations

For every skill, the compact Scope and Use when fields were parsed from the three registry documents. Soft-wrapped continuation lines were joined, and extraction failed if either field was missing. The skill identifier and deployment category were retained as metadata but were not included in the text to be embedded. The exact embedding input was therefore

Scope: <scope text>Use when: <use-when text>Each input was encoded with Qwen text-embedding-v4 using its default 1,024-dimensional output. Requests were made in batches of ten, and vectors were stored as a float32 matrix whose row order is fixed by embedding_index in skills.json. The deployed selector checks that the number of metadata rows equals the first dimension of the matrix before computing similarities. Because query and skill vectors must occupy the same vector space, the online query encoder is pinned to the same model; changing the embedding model requires regeneration of the entire matrix.

The embedding layer is used for task-to-skill seed retrieval, not as the sole definition of graph edges. This distinction is important: cosine proximity captures similarity between a requested need and the declared applicability of a skill, whereas it cannot by itself determine whether two skills substitute for one another, provide independent complementary evidence, or have a hard workflow prerequisite.

A.3.2 Exhaustive Pairwise Relationship and Dependency Scoring

All (1052)=5,460\binom{105}{2}=5,460 unordered skill pairs were evaluated. The judge received the complete SKILL.md bodies of Skill A and Skill B rather than the lossy compact registry records. It assigned five independent integer scores from 0 to 4, with fixed anchors, and one categorical dependency label. The symmetric relationship score was computed deterministically rather than requested from the model:

RA​B=PA​B+IA​B+SA​B+CA​B+JA​B,RA​B∈[0,20],R_{AB}=P_{AB}+I_{AB}+S_{AB}+C_{AB}+J_{AB},\qquad R_{AB}\in[0,20], (1)

where PP is purpose similarity, II is applicable-input overlap, SS is substitutability, CC is complementary gain from using both, and JJ is joint use or downstream joint consumption. The dimensions were scored independently: in particular, complementarity is not defined as the inverse of substitutability. The anchors and operational meanings are given in Table 4.

The dependency label was one of none, A_requires_B, B_requires_A or mutual. A direction was assigned only when using the dependent skill without first consulting or invoking the other would make its result unobtainable, incomplete or invalid—either because the other supplies a required input or because it supplies the rule under which the output must be interpreted. Merely helpful context, common co-use or higher confidence was not sufficient. Deployment class was hidden as a scoring signal so that same-directory pairs received no automatic advantage.

GPT-5.5 with high reasoning effort performed the scoring through a strict structured-output schema. The model returned the five subscores, dependency enum and a short rationale; Python validated ranges and types and summed the subscores. Calls used 32-way concurrency, exponential retry for transient/API failures (up to five attempts) and a separate structured-output validation retry (up to three attempts). Records were streamed to an append-only resumable JSONL file. The completed artefact contained all 5,460 pairs, no failed or duplicate pair, and no mutual dependency. Mean (s.d.) RR was 5.45 (2.99), the median was 5 and the observed range was 0–16. The 28 directed dependencies comprised 19 A_requires_B and nine B_requires_A labels.

The edge list was compiled into 105 node records. Every node stores (i) requires, its outgoing hard prerequisites; (ii) required_by, incoming hard dependencies; and (iii) all other 104 skills in related, sorted by decreasing RR and then by identifier, with the five subscores and dependency label retained for audit. Seventeen nodes have at least one outgoing prerequisite and 19 have at least one incoming dependency. Relationship bands were defined as strong (R=15R=15–20), moderate (R=8R=8–14), weak (R=1R=1–7) and none (R=0R=0); the deployed recall threshold deliberately includes both strong and moderate relationships.

A.3.3 Per-Message Seed Retrieval and Graph Expansion

Selection is recomputed once for every user message, including follow-up messages, rather than once for an entire session or once per internal tool call. The selector receives the current message plus at most the previous two question–answer pairs; each prior answer is truncated to 800 characters for this purpose. A fixed DeepSeek-V4-Flash decomposition step with thinking disabled returns strict JSON containing one to three short, non-overlapping English need statements. Each need must be expressed in the same objective register as a skill’s Scope/Use-when description and may represent phenotype normalization, a distinct variant type, gene–disease mechanism, or a requested classification task.

Each need is embedded independently with the pinned Qwen model. After L2L_{2} normalization, cosine similarity is calculated between all 105 skill vectors and each need vector. If EiE_{i} is the stored vector of skill ii and QkQ_{k} is need kk, the internal seed score is

si=maxk⁡Ei𝖳​Qk∥Ei∥2​∥Qk∥2.s_{i}=\max_{k}\frac{E_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}Q_{k}}{\lVert E_{i}\rVert_{2}\lVert Q_{k}\rVert_{2}}. (2)

The maximum, rather than a mean across needs, allows a specialized skill to be retained when it matches one facet of a multi-part request. The top n=30n=30 skills by sis_{i} form the seed set; no absolute cosine cutoff is applied in the deployed selector.

For each seed, all one-hop related edges with R≥x=8R\geq x=8 are added to a shared candidate pool. If a candidate is linked to more than one seed, only its largest edge score and the corresponding seed are retained. Candidates are ordered by decreasing edge score with identifier as the deterministic tie-breaker, and at most m=15m=15 are added. The expansion is intentionally one hop: newly expanded nodes do not themselves generate further similarity candidates. Independently, pubmed-search, pmc-search and tavily-search are always included because literature and official-web discovery are broadly useful; these forced skills do not act as expansion seeds. Finally, the outgoing requires list of every recalled node is traversed repeatedly until a fixed point is reached. Hard prerequisites are therefore included regardless of cosine rank, relationship threshold or the 15-skill expansion cap.

In compact form, if SS is the top-30 seed set, FF the three forced literature skills and T15T_{15} the operator retaining the 15 highest-scoring eligible candidates, the recalled set is

A0=S∪F∪T15​(⋃i∈S{j:Ri​j≥8}),A=closurerequires⁡(A0).A_{0}=S\cup F\cup T_{15}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in S}\{j:R_{ij}\geq 8\}\right),\qquad A=\operatorname{closure}_{\mathrm{requires}}(A_{0}). (3)

A.4 Details of the Automated Benchmark

A.4.1 Benchmark Composition and Case Construction

The benchmark used expert-curated records with discrete reference classifications and reconstructable public evidence. Eligible records were released or substantively updated after October 2025. For each case, the source identifier and version date, clinical input, supporting literature, reference answer, and scoring annotations were frozen before system evaluation. As the training-data cutoff dates of all evaluated models preceded October 2025, this temporal restriction ensured that the case-specific curation records and final reference classifications were held out from model training.

Supporting PMIDs were deduplicated within each source record and resolved to the local literature collection through PMID and DOI mappings. Available articles were converted to normalized plain text or Markdown while retaining headings and paragraph boundaries. Inclusion was assessed at the case level: the processed collection had to contain the public literature needed to reconstruct the reference answer. The same processed texts were supplied to every system, whereas source classifications, interpretation summaries, evidence scores and other ground-truth fields were stored separately and withheld.

For SNV interpretation, a public-evidence audit reduced 2,185 ClinGen expert-panel records to 1,683; requiring complete literature coverage yielded 300 eligible cases. Stratified sampling produced 79 cases (17 Pathogenic, 17 Likely Pathogenic, 17 Uncertain Significance, 12 Likely Benign and 16 Benign). The hidden reference retained the expert-panel classification, interpretation and criterion-level evidence annotations.

For gene–disease validity, up to 15 eligible ClinGen records were sampled per final class (fixed seed 42), with all records retained from smaller classes. The 66 cases comprised 15 Definitive, 10 Strong, 15 Moderate, 15 Limited, 2 No Known Disease Relationship, 6 Disputed and 3 Refuted relationships. Counted genetic and experimental points were summed from the structured ClinGen evidence tables, rounded to four decimal places and retained only as hidden reference annotations.

Clinical actionability retained the native source ontologies. The 46 CIViC cases comprised 20 Diagnostic, 12 Predictive, 10 Oncogenic, 3 Predisposing and 1 Prognostic assertions (33 with an applicable AMP category); the 12 OncoKB cases comprised four LEVEL_1, two LEVEL_2, four LEVEL_3A, one LEVEL_4 and one LEVEL_R2; and the 20 PharmGKB cases comprised one Level 1A, sixteen Level 3 and three Level 4. CIViC Diagnostic assertions were downsampled with seed 42; the other subsets were selected after source-specific eligibility filtering.

Reference-answer verification.

Reference answers were inherited from versioned source records and were not model-generated. Three physicians with more than five years of relevant experience reviewed all 223 cases for entity–record correspondence, reference-label and annotation accuracy, literature coverage, ground-truth leakage, anonymization and agreement between the task and scoring schema. Ambiguities were resolved before freezing, and system outputs did not alter the references. Only spelling, capitalization, whitespace and unambiguous aliases were normalized across databases.

A.4.2 System Inputs, Output Schemas and Execution Protocol

All systems received the same case-level clinical entities, task instructions and processed literature, with no cross-case history. Ground-truth fields were withheld; direct access to the five source databases was prohibited. Individual papers were limited to 80,000 characters and combined literature to 200,000 characters. System configurations are given in Supplementary Table 7.

Because some systems provided their own search or database tools, we additionally used an LLM to audit each complete execution record for substantive case-specific information obtained from the corresponding reference resource, either directly or indirectly through an intermediary. Mere mention of a resource or use of general framework terminology was not counted. Positive records were uncommon for every system and task (Supplementary Table 6).

The common case-facing instruction layer is reproduced below. Framework-specific tool-calling scaffolds differed, but clinical fields, literature and required outputs were controlled across systems.

The system-specific execution controls recorded in the archived harnesses are summarized in Supplementary Table 8. Free-text answers were subsequently converted into task-specific structured fields by a fixed extraction pipeline. Missing or unrecognized fields were retained as null values rather than repaired from the reference answer.

Final-classification and evidence metrics were computed from the frozen single-output records described below. The repeated-run consistency and per-case wall-clock time reported in the main figure were obtained through a separate repetition-and-timing workflow and were not derived from those single-output metric files.

A.4.3 Metric Implementation and Denominators

All reported classification and evidence metrics were recomputed from the frozen structured reference data and extracted system outputs by deterministic code. The denominators differ by task and, in two cases, by endpoint; they are summarized in Supplementary Table 9. No LLM judge determined whether a final classification matched the reference.

A.4.4 SNV-Specific Evaluation Metrics

Final-classification concordance required an exact five-tier match. Pathogenic/Likely Pathogenic and Benign/Likely Benign formed the positive and negative groups for sensitivity and specificity; VUS cases were excluded. A significant error was a direction reversal between these groups and used all 79 cases as its denominator.

For reference criterion set EiE_{i} and recovered set E^i\hat{E}_{i}, micro recall was ∑i|Ei∩E^i|/∑i|Ei|\sum_{i}|E_{i}\cap\hat{E}_{i}|/\sum_{i}|E_{i}| and macro recall was the mean case-level recall; the micro value is the weighted evidence recall reported in the main figure. A criterion counted only when asserted as met for the evaluated variant–disease pair. Strength concordance required exact strength agreement among correctly recovered criteria.

A.4.5 Gene–Disease Validity-Specific Evaluation Metrics

The fixed ranks were Refuted =−2=-2, Disputed =−1=-1, No Known Disease Relationship =0=0, Limited =1=1, Moderate =2=2, Strong =3=3 and Definitive =4=4. Concordance and rank differences used parsable seven-category outputs; differences of at least two levels defined primary severe over- or under-classification (three levels in supplementary analyses).

Evidence “coverage” denotes reporting of a usable genetic or experimental score, not item-level recall. Reference scores were capped at 12 and 6 points, respectively. For an extracted interval [Li,Hi][L_{i},H_{i}] and reference gig_{i}, error was max⁡(0,Li−gi,gi−Hi)\max(0,L_{i}-g_{i},g_{i}-H_{i}); MAE was conditional on a stated score, with no imputation.

A.4.6 Clinical Actionability-Specific Evaluation Metrics

Final-classification concordance used the 65 cases with an applicable tier: CIViC AMP category, OncoKB level or PharmGKB level. Complete-answer accuracy used all 78 cases and required, respectively, CIViC assertion type/significance/direction and applicable AMP category; OncoKB level and exact drug set; or PharmGKB level and a score within 0.5 points of reference.

Severity analyses used the source-specific ranks in Supplementary Table 10. A rank difference of at least two levels defined primary severe over- or under-classification (three levels in supplementary analyses); missing or unmappable labels remained in the fixed 65-case denominator.

The placement of OncoKB resistance categories is an analysis convention rather than an official crosswalk: LEVEL_R1 was aligned with standard-care evidence at rank 5 and LEVEL_R2 with emerging clinical evidence at rank 3. This convention was fixed in the evaluator before system comparison.

Rule-based scoring and missing outputs.

All matches were determined from parsed outputs and frozen references using rules fixed before comparison; the extraction model only normalized labels, criteria and numerical intervals. Missing SNV and actionability predictions remained incorrect in fixed denominators, whereas unparsable gene–disease predictions were reported separately and excluded from concordance and severity denominators. Supplementary Table 9 gives all endpoint-specific denominators.

A.4.7 Blinded Clinician Assessment of Report Quality

Nine clinicians rated the reports from ClinGeX, Biomni and DeepResearch for all 223 cases. Six clinicians with more than three years of genetic-analysis experience reviewed SNV or gene–disease reports; three internal-medicine physicians with more than five years of experience reviewed clinical-actionability reports.

Within each task, cases were partitioned among three reviewers (SNV: 27/26/26; gene–disease: 22/22/22; actionability: 27/26/25), with no duplicate rating. The assigned reviewer assessed all three reports for a case. Report identities were independently permuted to Result A–C for each case and revealed only after export.

Each report received eight ordered three-category ratings without a not-applicable option: six common dimensions (Supplementary Table 11) and two task-specific dimensions (Supplementary Table 12).

Completion and aggregation.

All cases were complete: 669 reports and 5,352 ordinal ratings, with no missing value or imputation. After de-blinding, category counts and proportions were summarized by task, system and dimension. No composite score was defined; inter-rater agreement was not estimated because cases were partitioned rather than multiply rated. These ratings neither altered the references nor entered the automated metrics.

A.5 Selection of the System Architecture

A.5.1 Study Objective and Controlled Comparison

This experiment compared the complete ClinGeX architecture with an unenhanced DeepSeek-V4 baseline and five single-strategy enhancements on evidence-grounded question–answering items. DeepSeek-V4, item text and hidden-reference controls were held fixed, so conditions differed only in the enhancement or orchestration layer listed in Supplementary Table 13. Unlike the 223-case end-to-end benchmark, this dataset isolated specific evidence-reasoning operations.

A.5.2 Implementation of the Seven Framework Conditions

Supplementary Table 13 defines the seven conditions. The RAG condition exposed only the search-facing functions from the ClinGeX library; few-shot used the same three fixed demonstrations for every item; and the multi-agent condition used sequential planner, executor and reviewer roles. BioSkill (https://github.com/GPTomics/bioSkills) and MedSkill (https://github.com/aipoch/medical-research-skills) were frozen snapshots exposed through the same discovery-and-load wrapper without adding ClinGeX content or graph edges. The full ClinGeX condition retained its native skill selection, dependency expansion and progressive execution workflow. No condition received the hidden reference answer or scoring rubric.

A.5.3 Benchmark Construction

The benchmark drew from ClinVar, ClinGen, CIViC, OncoKB and ClinPGx. Eighty diversity-oriented anchors were selected deterministically: 10 each from OncoKB and CIViC and 20 each from ClinPGx, ClinVar and ClinGen. Selection favoured distinct genes and, where applicable, literature-supported pathogenic assertions or ClinGen records with both genetic and experimental evidence and non-trivial scoring or mechanistic issues.

DeepSeek-V4 generated items in 240 independent anchor–tier jobs using source- and tier-specific instructions, structured records and linked full text; related records could be retrieved for clinically plausible comparisons or distractors. Retained items had to pose a meaningful clinical operation, have a literature-verifiable answer and require interpretation rather than copying. Schema validation required a source-grounded answer, numeric PMIDs with relevance labels, at least one relevant PMID, a construction rationale and an item-level rubric. The final 426 items are summarized in Supplementary Table 14.

A.5.4 Reasoning Tiers and Task-Specific Construction Rules

Tiers were defined by the required evidence operation, as specified in Supplementary Table 15. Tier 1 items used no deliberately irrelevant PMID and cited a mean of 1.19 publications. Tier 2 allowed realistic non-supporting evidence when available (43/124 items; mean 2.82 publications). Tier 3 integrated multiple sources (mean 4.93 publications) and comprised 51 easy, 27 medium and 27 hard items according to evidence volume, conflict and irrelevant context.

A.5.5 Response Generation and Rubric-Based Evaluation

All seven conditions answered the same 426 frozen prompts with DeepSeek-V4 as the common core. Reference answers, construction rationales, PMID relevance labels and rubrics were withheld. GPT-5.5 and Claude-4.8-Opus independently scored each source-masked response against its item-specific rubric; factual errors, omissions, irrelevant evidence, over-claiming and clinically incorrect recommendations reduced credit. The complete shared judge prompt follows.

Let ri​j​mr_{ijm} be the rubric points awarded to framework mm on item ii by judge jj, and RiR_{i} the item maximum. The primary rubric-normalised score was

Sm=100×1N∑i=1N12(ri,GPT,mRi+ri,Claude,mRi).S_{m}=100\times\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{r_{i,\mathrm{GPT},m}}{R_{i}}+\frac{r_{i,\mathrm{Claude},m}}{R_{i}}\right). (4)

Each item therefore contributed equally, regardless of rubric length or publication count. The same mean was calculated by reasoning tier and clinical-genomics domain; it measures rubric-defined factual correctness, evidence selection and weighting, completeness and final synthesis rather than exact-match accuracy.

A.5.6 Framework-Selection Result

The full ClinGeX architecture achieved the highest rubric-normalised score overall and in every reasoning tier (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Its overall score was 83.2%, compared with 72.2% for the unenhanced DeepSeek-V4 baseline and 74.0–78.4% for the five single-strategy conditions. The largest separation occurred for tier 3 synthesis tasks. ClinGeX scored 70.1% on variant-interpretation items, 56.7% on gene–disease-validity items and 84.9% on clinical-actionability items, corresponding to improvements of 15.2, 11.1 and 15.1 percentage points, respectively, over the same base model without an enhancement layer. These controlled comparisons supported selection of the complete skill-centred architecture for the main system evaluation.

A.6 Selection of the Frontier LLM Used as the Agent Core

A.6.1 Purpose and Experimental Design

This experiment changed only the LLM core while holding the complete ClinGeX architecture, skills, tools, instructions and 3,662-item input set fixed. It compared the six frontier models in Supplementary Table 16 across variant interpretation (n=1,366n=1{,}366), gene–disease validity (n=1,253n=1{,}253) and clinical actionability (n=1,043n=1{,}043). Candidate cores were excluded from external judging.

A.6.2 Source Records and Construction of the Evidence-Grounded QA Corpus

The six pipelines used ClinVar and ClinGen-ACMG for variant interpretation, ClinGen Gene–Disease Validity for gene–disease assessment, and CIViC, OncoKB and PharmGKB/ClinPGx for clinical actionability. Every item was joined to a processed publication at the finest PMID-linked evidence unit supported by its source schema. Multi-publication narratives were treated only as trust anchors; claims and evidence codes had to be verified in the current paper, preventing cross-paper leakage or attribution to a comparator allele, disease, drug or population.

Source-specific candidate, acceptance and final-inclusion counts are given in Supplementary Table 17. The frozen experiment contained 3,662 items: 1,366 variant-interpretation, 1,253 gene–disease-validity and 1,043 clinical-actionability items.

A.6.3 Adversarial QA Generation and Quality Control

A source-specific generator produced a publication-grounded question, reference answer, reasoning annotation and supporting quotations. Items had to require interpretation or synthesis, and every quotation had to fuzzy-match the current full text at a similarity of at least 0.80.

Four memoryless answerers (DeepSeek-V4, Qwen3.7-Max, MiniMax-M3 and MiMo-V2.5-Pro) then answered from the same paper. A source-masked Qwen3.7-Plus arbiter from a different model family checked ambiguity, source support, overreach and semantic difficulty, returning discriminative acceptance, consensus-hard acceptance or rejection. Rejected units were regenerated for at most three quality attempts. Accepted audit records were retained but hidden from evaluated cores.

A.6.4 Model-Facing Input, Leakage Control and Common Workflow

Each core received the question and retrieval entry points, not full text in the initial prompt, and used the same ClinGeX skills, tool definitions, 50-turn limit, timeout and retry policy. Runs retained the final answer, status and complete trace, including tool, skill, action, canonical parameters and result metadata.

Construction answerers, arbitration data, rejected attempts, generator rationale and target reasoning point were removed before inference; reference answers, quotations and source annotations were scoring-only. Every (model, item) pair was run independently three times without shared state, retrieved content or tool history.

A.6.5 Five Evaluation Dimensions

The five dimensions combined external-judge assessment of the response with judge-free analysis of the execution trace. The external judge was not one of the six candidate cores.

Absolute accuracy.

Each reference answer was cached as atomic claims. The item score was 1 when all claims were supported, 0.5 when at least half were supported, and 0 otherwise; contradiction of the critical target claim forced a score of 0. Thus, accuracy was a deterministic 0/0.5/1 claim-coverage score rather than string matching.

Reasoning score.

Five binary indicators assessed specific evidence use, recognition of the hidden reasoning issue, logical connection of evidence to conclusion, coverage of all requested parts and consistency between rationale and answer. Their sum ranged from 0 to 5.

Agentic ability.

Three judge-free trace statistics captured execution effort and reliability: tool-call count TT, failed-call rate ff and exact-duplicate rate dd, where duplicates shared the same skill, action and canonical parameters. Values were averaged across the three runs and, for multi-source domains, across sources with equal weight. For the radar axis, each statistic was reverse min–max normalized across the six models within a domain and combined as Gm=(Zm,T+Zm,f+Zm,d)/3G_{m}=(Z_{m,T}+Z_{m,f}+Z_{m,d})/3. Raw statistics were retained because call count alone was not interpreted as quality.

Faithfulness.

Direct quotations were fuzzy-matched to retrieved text; other concrete claims were labelled supported, contradicted or unverifiable against retrieved evidence. With fabricated-quotation rate qiq_{i} and contradicted-or-unverifiable factual-claim rate hih_{i}, faithfulness was Hi=1−0.5​qi−0.5​hiH_{i}=1-0.5q_{i}-0.5h_{i}. Errors affecting key values, evidence levels, clinical scope or conclusions were additionally flagged as high severity.

Robustness.

Across three independent runs, answer consistency CiC_{i} was 1 when all accuracy scores agreed, 0.5 when two agreed and 0 otherwise. Tool-sequence similarity UiU_{i} was the mean pairwise Levenshtein similarity of (skill, action) sequences; agentic stability ViV_{i} was one minus the mean coefficient of variation of tool, failed and duplicate-call counts, truncated at zero. The composite was Bi=0.4​Ci+0.3​Ui+0.3​ViB_{i}=0.4C_{i}+0.3U_{i}+0.3V_{i}.

A.6.6 External Judge Prompt

Reference claims were decomposed once per item and reused for every model and run. The source-masked prompt below separately elicits claim correctness, five reasoning indicators and factual-faithfulness labels; candidate models never received the reference-only fields.

The scoring code validated the returned schema, summed the five reasoning indicators, applied the deterministic accuracy thresholds and combined the faithfulness labels with the independent quotation-matching result. The judge was not given the candidate model name.

A.7 Details of the MRMC Human-AI Collaboration Study

The details below supplement the main study design. The analysis unit was a submitted case assessment; reader-facing materials never contained reference answers, scoring annotations or adjudication records.

A.7.1 Dedicated Online Evaluation Platform

The password-protected platform linked each account to nine fixed task–condition assignments and presented de-identified case materials beside the scenario-specific response form. Reference answers, scoring keys, other readers’ responses and alternate-condition responses to the same case were inaccessible. Readers used no AI in the unassisted condition or consulted the assigned external DeepSeek/ClinGeX interface before entering their own conclusion; AI output was never copied automatically.

Drafts were retained, required fields were checked on submission and oncology readers completed the open response before viewing candidate statements. Completion time was self-reported rather than inferred from browser duration. Scenario fields are listed in Supplementary Table 18; five-level confidence was encoded 1–5 from no confidence to very confident.

A.7.2 Reference Standards and Expert Adjudication

Before analysis, each three-member scenario panel froze a reference record matching the reader fields: final classification, ACMG/AMP criteria and strengths for criterion-level variant analysis; candidate pathogenicity, phenotype explanation and acceptable adjacent levels for genomic interpretation in rare disease; and a core open answer plus graded candidate statements for molecular oncology decision-making. Enumerated fields were compared by prespecified mappings, while free text and borderline cases were resolved by source-masked panel consensus based on clinical equivalence rather than wording or response length.

Primary outcome: case-level overall concordance.

For each scenario and condition, concordance was the proportion of the 45 submitted assessments satisfying the complete task-specific rule in Supplementary Table 19; no pooled primary outcome combined the three scenarios.

A.7.3 Secondary Performance Outcomes

Secondary outcomes isolated the structured reasoning components listed with their units and denominators in Supplementary Table 20; eligible item instances were micro-averaged within condition.

For criterion-level variant analysis, evidence recall was ∑i|Gi∩Pi|/∑i|Gi|\sum_{i}|G_{i}\cap P_{i}|/\sum_{i}|G_{i}|, unsupported-evidence assignment was ∑i|Pi∖Gi|/∑i|Pi|\sum_{i}|P_{i}\setminus G_{i}|/\sum_{i}|P_{i}|, and strength concordance required an exact strength match among recalled reference criteria. The second metric is labelled the evidence hallucination rate in the figure and code, but denotes an unsupported ACMG/AMP criterion rather than a fabricated citation. Final-class accuracy and directional over-/underestimation used the ordered five-tier pathogenicity scale; the reference contained 176 criterion instances.

For genomic interpretation in rare disease, the 117 candidate variants were evaluated for exact pathogenicity, directional error and phenotype-explanation accuracy. Phenotype accuracy allowed an accepted adjacent level only when the substantive interpretation was preserved; over-/underestimation was measured beyond this accepted range. Primary concordance additionally required the correct causal combination and inheritance interpretation.

For molecular oncology decision-making, free-response accuracy used panel-adjudicated agreement with the core answer across 45 cases. The four statements per case produced 180 judgements; accuracy required the reference clinical position, while over-/underestimation followed the ordered unreasonable–partly reasonable–basically reasonable scale and did not tolerate a supported–unsupported boundary crossing.

A.7.4 Confidence–Correctness Alignment, Time, Survey and Continued-Use Outcomes

For criterion-level variant analysis, behavioural certainty was full when all 28 ACMG/AMP criteria had an explicit applicable/not-applicable call and partial when any remained undetermined. Group accuracy used exact final pathogenicity classification, not the stricter primary composite; Wilson intervals were descriptive because fully certain groups were small.

For genomic interpretation in rare disease, correctness was primary case-level concordance; for molecular oncology decision-making, it was correctness of the open answer entered immediately before confidence. Five-level confidence was related to correctness using point-biserial correlation and ROC–AUC. Positive correlation and AUC above 0.5 indicate discrimination.

Confidence categories were mapped to probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9 for the Brier score, N−1​∑i(qi−Yi)2N^{-1}\sum_{i}(q_{i}-Y_{i})^{2}; correlation and AUC retained the original ordinal scores. Expected calibration error was descriptive, with no model fitting or threshold optimization.

The main time comparison used each reader’s post-study estimate of mean minutes per case, not browser-open duration or the case-form field. Paired two-sided Wilcoxon tests within scenario were Holm-adjusted, and medians were reported.

The questionnaire comprised three time items and five ordinal dimensions rated separately for DeepSeek and ClinGeX; ratings were summarized by mean and standard deviation. Continued use was the number of new ClinGeX conversations initiated in the 14 days after completion, excluding three assigned study sessions, and was analysed descriptively without hypothesis testing.

A.7.5 Statistical Analysis of Proportions and Effect Differences

Observed numerators and denominators were retained for descriptive reporting. For each scenario and outcome, condition effects were estimated using a binomial logistic GLMM with condition as a fixed effect and crossed random intercepts for reader and case. Case-level binary outcomes were entered as success or failure; item-level outcomes were grouped within each reader–case assessment as cbind(success, total-success), thereby retaining their observed denominators. Accuracy, overestimation and underestimation were analysed as separate binary outcomes. Model-standardized probabilities and absolute between-condition differences in percentage points were obtained by integrating over the estimated reader- and case-level random-effect distributions, with two-sided 95% Wald confidence intervals. For outcomes where lower values were favourable, figures show one minus the model-standardized event probability and the direction of each contrast was reversed. Pairwise Wald contrasts were Holm-adjusted across the three comparisons within each outcome and scenario; the corresponding two-degree-of-freedom omnibus Wald test was descriptive only. Random slopes were not fitted because each reader contributed only three assessments per condition within a scenario.

A.7.6 Representative Complete Reader-Facing Tasks

The following examples reproduce the structure and level of information presented to readers. They are shown without participant answers and without the hidden expert scoring record.

A.7.7 Construction and Quality Control of the Molecular Oncology Tasks

The 323 human molecular-oncology case reports identified in the main Methods—186 digestive-system and 137 thoracic-tumour reports published after 2025—were processed independently before expert selection. GPT-5.5 read each complete report and returned structured fields comprising the clinically decisive or counterintuitive features, their clinical implication, a de-identified vignette, one direct question, a concise core answer and explicit scoring points. Vignettes retained the clinical, pathological, treatment and molecular facts needed to answer the question, but omitted article titles, authors, journals, identifiers and source-revealing wording.

Five independent models—DeepSeek-V4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, GLM-5.1 and Qwen3.7—then answered each vignette and question in fresh contexts without access to the report, reference answer or other model responses. Claude Opus 4.8 subsequently assessed whether the reference was source-grounded and clinically defensible; whether the vignette was self-contained and free of answer or publication leakage; whether the question was single, direct and appropriate for a practising oncologist; and whether the simulated responses demonstrated useful discriminatory difficulty. Failed items were regenerated by GPT-5.5 using the arbitrator’s written feedback and rerun through independent answering and arbitration, for at most five generation rounds. Reports without an acceptable task were discarded.

For each accepted open question, the reference conclusion supplied the best-supported of four candidate statements, while incorrect or partially correct model responses were used to construct clinically plausible alternatives. Each statement received a hidden five-point truth grade: grades 4–5 mapped to basically reasonable, grade 3 to partly reasonable, and grades 1–2 to unreasonable. Statement order was randomized. A final validation pass required consistency between the core answer and statement grades, exactly one best-supported statement, defensible distractors and no superficial answer cue from length, tone, certainty or absolute wording. The reader-facing task contained only the vignette, question and statements; source reports, scoring points, truth grades, simulated answers and revision records were retained separately for audit and adjudication.

The automated pipeline produced 36 digestive-system and 26 thoracic-tumour candidates. A three-member oncology panel completed and reviewed every candidate for clinical relevance, objectivity, answer defensibility, difficulty, actionability, leakage risk and the plausibility and grading of all statements. The panel retained 27 digestive-system and 18 thoracic-tumour tasks, yielding the final 45, and could correct the core answer, statement wording or reference grades before the scoring record was frozen. Finally, the selected vignettes were manually de-identified: nonessential details and publication-revealing phrases were removed or reformulated, but no fact required to answer the clinical question was deleted.

A.8 Feedback Coverage in the Prospective Deployment

To assess the completeness of episode-level feedback, we counted all platform conversations recorded for each participant during the deployment period. A conversation was one platform session and could contain multiple dialogue turns. Feedback was submitted per completed analysis episode, and one episode could span multiple conversations. To preserve participant privacy, we did not inspect conversation content and therefore could not determine whether conversations without associated feedback were outside the study scope or represented eligible episodes for which feedback was not submitted. We therefore treated the ratio of feedback submissions to conversations as a conservative lower-bound proxy for episode-level feedback coverage, rather than as a one-to-one response rate. Overall, 96 feedback submissions were recorded for 111 conversations (86.5%); participant-level ratios ranged from 66.7% to 100% (Supplementary Table 21). This high lower-bound coverage was consistent with participants generally following the requested feedback procedure.
